findings.question: Actual AR acceptance to first R delay, per-child vs per-word service, maximum outstanding/queue entries/per-ID order, RR update from real handshake, held RVALID behavior. Is there a real charged serial first-beat/setup delay for each extra source AR or only possible overlap?
findings.answer: In the supplied actual-DMA SYSTEM C++ model, every accepted shared-DDR AR becomes one MemRead entry with len = burst beats and latency = ptw_latency, sampled with accepted_cycle = g_cycle. The DDR R driver services only mem_q.front(). In the default serial latency mode it decrements only the head entry's latency and returns until that head latency reaches zero, then emits one R beat per R handshake. A later queued AR does not have its latency decremented until it becomes the head. Therefore there is a charged serial first-beat/setup delay per accepted AR transaction/child by default, not a per-word delay. This is a C++ behavioral shared-DDR model delay, not measured RTL/hardware cycles. Main default ptw_lat is 31, and the test explicitly prints that ptw latency is a plain model delay, NOT MIG-matched. Optional +read-latency-model=overlap changes the head check to accepted_cycle + h.latency and can let another ID rotate to the head only when optional interleave is enabled. Maximum model entries: ddr_ar_ready accepts while mem_q.size() < 16, so at most 16 accepted shared-DDR read entries in this model. Crossbar config also has MaxMstTrans=8 and MaxSlvTrans=8, and each dma_core_wrap has NumAxInFlight=8. Per-ID order: optional rotation searches for the first (oldest) entry of a candidate full AXI ID, so same-ID AR order is preserved within the model. RR cursor r_rr_last_id is updated only on an actual f_ddr_r R handshake under the optional interleave/overlap/phase condition. Held RVALID: the interval gate is skipped when ddr_r_held is true and is documented never to suppress an already held VALID.

findings.question: How PTW read responses and payload R arbitrate; can one PTE R occur between payload beats of an unfinished source burst, rather than only after source RLAST? Bank knobs/defaults/select-ID/interval/delay and source-AR serialization.
findings.answer: The supplied SYSTEM C++ model has ONE ordered shared-DDR R-return queue mem_q. Payload reads from the completion master are counted as top-ID-class 2; DS/PTW reads are top-ID-class 3. By default there is no mid-burst promotion: ds_priority defaults false, memory_r_interleave defaults 0, read_latency_overlap defaults false, memory_r_interval defaults 0, and memory_b_delay defaults 0. drive_ddr() always takes mem_q.front() as the head and returns one R beat per R handshake, popping only when h.beat == h.len. Therefore by default a PTW/PTE R cannot occur between payload beats of an unfinished source burst; it can only be served after the current head payload burst RLAST or when no payload head is selected. Optional non-default model knobs can change this: +ds-priority=1 promotes the oldest DS request to the head while win_open and no R beat is held, which can interrupt a payload burst mid-beat; +memory-r-interleave=1 with +read-latency-model=overlap and an active phase rotates the next ready distinct full AXI ID to the head at a beat boundary, and can select a PTE/DS ID if it is eligible. The select-ID RR cursor is a 6-bit full AXI ID and advances only on an actual R handshake. The interval gate is global across all DDR IDs and only suppresses a new VALID; it never withdraws an already held VALID. Source-AR serialization by default follows the same head-only FIFO, so extra source ARs queue behind the current head and are not independently serviced unless one of the optional non-default promotions/interleave knobs is enabled.

findings.question: Existing fixture successful translation/grant APIs: owner/prepare/access_ok result output? Raw PA/raw IOTLB or AW hot/cold gates; identify which are native actual vs proposed missing prepare/owned-result route; can old source READ range be reused without forced PTE?
findings.answer: In the supplied parent_translation_reuse fixture there is NO explicit access_ok output. The fixture stores a normal TL response payload containing error, ignore, spaddr, is_mrif, range, bypass, fault_code, w/r/x/sum/g/u/t2gpa. The successful usable gate is cache_valid_o, which requires enable_i, no flush, parent_valid_i, matching seq_q, !error, !ignore, !is_mrif, and either the stored write/read permission or bypass. Raw PA output is cache_pa_o = value_q[f][n].spaddr. There is a cache_failed_o output for prepared-but-not-valid entries. prepare_i triggers a real forwarded preparation request; on m_valid_o && m_ready_i with prep_offer_q the fixture sets prepared_q and records seq_q, and only on a later m_resp_valid_i && m_resp_ready_o with a successful response (!error, !ignore, !is_mrif, spaddr[11:0] == iova[11:0]) does it set valid_q and store the normal response. Owner is internal slow_owner_q / reuse_owner / first_owner, not a public output. The supplied module header says this is a prototype for static normal mappings only and does not establish fault, invalidation or epoch semantics. Thus cache_valid_o/cache_pa_o are actual supplied fixture outputs, but the stage86 root card explicitly states that a native successful prepare handshake / access_ok / owned trusted-PA result route is proposed and not existing current production interface. Raw IOTLB and AW hot/cold observation taps do exist: dbg_tl_iotlb_lookup = tl_e3.lookup, dbg_tl_iotlb_hit = tl_e3.hit, dbg_iotlb_fill, dbg_tr_aw_stall, and dbg_aw_wait_flags. C++ also has v_cold_dst and owner_only gates. For old source READ range reuse without forced PTE: stage85-b says the split derives the second AR3 only inside the already-owned source READ range, normal native/range reuse, and does not force a new READ PTW. The supplied fixture's reuse condition can reuse a cached parent if the child IOVA matches the parent key or is parent key + 1024 within the same 4K page, or if prepare_i and iova == k.iova, so the prototype also supports same-page reuse without a new walk. This is prototype/hand-contract evidence, not proof that current production already exposes the required prepare/owned-result route.

findings.question: Minimum cost facts which support/refute stage85 hand continuous-source-R vs PTE-after-RLAST service model; do not promote hypothetical AR-energy weight to actual cycles, and do not conclude all hardware lacks it.
findings.answer: Stage85-b explicitly defines its time model as an abstract discrete service hand case, not RTL cycles. Its external_R common contract says one selected source child has ordered R until its RLAST, PTW R can be inserted between source children, source FIFO backpressure causes stalls, and PTE order follows actual legal requests; it does not force all split tail grants to be ready first. That contract is consistent with the supplied default C++ mem_q behavior: the head payload entry is serviced until h.beat == h.len, so by default a PTE/PTW R is served after the current payload burst RLAST or when no payload head is selected, not between its beats. However, the supplied C++ model also has non-default ds_priority and memory_r_interleave/read_latency_overlap options that can promote DS/PTE to the head or rotate another ID to the head at a beat boundary. Therefore the supplied evidence supports the stage85 hand model as a selected legal/default service contract, but it does not support the stronger claim that all hardware lacks PTE-between-payload-beats service. On cost: stage85-b defines e_AR as a hardware command/energy/resource price that must be measured or estimated, not automatically equal to RTL cycles; its e_AR=3 vs e_AR=1 numeric cases are explanatory cost-unit examples, not measurements. The stage86 root candidate card states the source setup price in the stage85 economic objective was an abstract weight, not actual RTL or hardware measured latency. The supplied C++ model does have a per-request ptw_latency setup, default 31, but the test itself labels it a plain model delay, NOT MIG-matched. Thus these files refute promoting the hypothetical AR-energy weight to actual cycles, and they do not justify concluding that real hardware cannot interleave a PTE R between payload beats.
